ta-l1d8q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus opening Distinction 8. Having shown the Trinity in the unity of essence, Lombard now treats what pertains to each. There are three things in God: the common essence, the distinct person, and the distinguishing property. He treats them first in themselves, the essence (Dist. 8), the persons (Dist. 9 onward), and the properties (Dist. 26 onward), and then in their mutual relations (Dist. 33 onward). The treatment of the essence follows three attributes: its truth or unity, its immutability, and its simplicity. Lombard first shows the truth of the divine essence and then removes a doubt about Jerome's words. On the propriety of divine being Thomas poses two inquiries, on divine being itself and on its measure, eternity. The first has three articles: whether being properly belongs to God, whether his being is the being of every creature, and how the name 'He who is' ranks among divine names.
claims: In God there are three things to consider: common essence, distinct person, and distinguishing property.
Lombard treats the divine essence under the attributes of truth, immutability, and simplicity.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e131.summary: First objection that being is not said properly of God. What is proper to something belongs to it alone, and being belongs to creatures as well as God.
claims: What is proper belongs to one alone.
concepts: being common to God and creatures

ta-l1d8q1-d1e134.summary: Second objection. We can name God only as we know him (Damascene: the word is the intellect's messenger), and in this life we know him only from creatures. 'He who is' implies no relation to creatures, so it does not properly name God.
claims: We name God only as we know him, from creatures.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e140.summary: Third objection. Created being falls short of uncreated being as created wisdom falls short of uncreated wisdom. 'Wisdom' falls short of perfectly signifying God's wisdom because we impose it from created wisdom, so 'He who is' likewise falls short and is no more proper than other names.
claims: Names imposed from creatures fall short of signifying God perfectly.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e144.summary: Fourth objection. Damascene says 'He who is' signifies not what God is but an infinite ocean of substance. The infinite is incomprehensible and therefore unnameable and unknown.
claims: The infinite is incomprehensible and unnameable.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e150.summary: Sed contra from Exodus 3:14 ('He who is has sent me to you'), from Damascene, who calls 'He who is' the most proper name of God, and from Maimonides, who calls it God's ineffable name, held most worthy.
claims: Scripture, Damascene, and Maimonides treat 'He who is' as God's most proper name.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e159.summary: Thomas's determination: 'He who is' is the most proper of God's names, for four reasons. (1) From Jerome, on the perfection of divine being: the perfect is that of which nothing is outside it. Our being has something of itself outside itself, the past that has gone and the future to come, but in divine being nothing is past or future, so God has his whole being perfectly and being belongs to him properly. (2) From Damascene: 'He who is' signifies being indeterminately, not what God is. In this life we know only that God is and know what he is only by negation, and we name as we know, so 'He who is' names him most properly. (3) From Dionysius: being is first among all participations of divine goodness (living, understanding) and their principle, containing them all in a unified way, as God is the principle in whom all are one. (4) From Avicenna: in everything there is a quiddity, by which it subsists in a determinate nature, and its being, by which it is in act. 'Thing' (res) is imposed from quiddity, 'He who is' or 'being' (ens) from the act of being. Since in every creature essence differs from being, a creature is properly named from its quiddity ('man' from humanity). In God being is his quiddity, so the name taken from being is his proper name.
claims: 'He who is' is the most proper name of God.
God's being is perfect because nothing of it is past or future.
In this life we know that God is, not what he is, so the name of indeterminate being suits him best.
Since God's being is his quiddity, the name taken from being is properly his.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e168.summary: Reply to the first objection. Something is said to belong 'properly' in two ways. In one way the property excludes whatever is foreign to the subject's nature, as risibility is proper to humans; in this sense being is not proper to God, since it belongs to creatures too. In the other way it excludes whatever is foreign to the predicate's nature, as gold is properly gold when unmixed with another metal; in this sense being is proper to God, since divine being has no admixture of privation or potentiality, as creaturely being does. That is why Lombard's text uses 'propriety' and 'truth' interchangeably: true gold is gold unmixed with anything foreign.
claims: Being is proper to God not as belonging to him alone but as unmixed with privation or potentiality.
Propriety in this sense coincides with truth, as in 'true gold'.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e171.summary: Reply to the second objection. God is named from creatures in three ways. (1) The name connotes an effect in creatures by an implied relation (Creator, Lord). (2) The name signifies, by its concept, the principle of a divine act in creatures (wisdom, power, will). (3) The name signifies something represented in creatures (living, since all life is modelled on divine life). 'He who is' names God in the third way, through the being found in creatures, which derives exemplarily from him.
claims: God is named from creatures by connoted effects, by principles of action, or by exemplary representation.
'He who is' names God through creaturely being as exemplarily derived from him.
concepts: modes of naming God from creatures

ta-l1d8q1-d1e177.summary: Reply to the third objection. Since creaturely being represents divine being imperfectly, 'He who is' signifies God imperfectly, by way of concretion and composition. Other names signify him even more imperfectly. 'God is wise' includes being and so has a twofold imperfection: that of concrete being, as in 'He who is', and in addition that of the concept of wisdom, since created wisdom falls short of divine wisdom. So the other names are more imperfect, and 'He who is' is worthier and more proper to God.
claims: 'He who is' signifies God imperfectly, but less imperfectly than other names, which add a further deficiency.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. All other names signify determinate and particularized being ('wise' signifies being something), but 'He who is' signifies being absolute and undetermined by anything added. Hence Damascene says it signifies an infinite ocean of substance, as undetermined. In the way of remotion we first deny bodily things of God, then intellectual things as found in creatures, such as goodness and wisdom, and only 'that he is' remains, in a kind of confusion. Finally we remove even being as it is in creatures, and there remains a darkness of ignorance in which, as far as this life goes, we are best joined to God (Dionysius). This is the cloud in which God is said to dwell.
claims: 'He who is' signifies being absolute and undetermined, unlike other names.
The way of remotion ends by removing even creaturely being, leaving a darkness of ignorance in which we are best united to God in this life.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e205.summary: First argument that God is the being of all things, from Dionysius: the being of all things is the super-being of the divinity, and God himself is being for existing things.
claims: Dionysius calls God the being of existing things.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e214.summary: Second argument. No creature exists through itself but through another, yet being is not through another, or the same question would arise about that other to infinity. So being is uncaused and is God.
claims: Being cannot be through another without infinite regress.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e217.summary: Third argument. Things that exist and in no way differ are the same. God and the being of a thing exist and do not differ, since whatever differs does so by some difference and so is composite, while being and God are both simple.
claims: Whatever differs does so by a difference and is composite.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e221.summary: Sed contra. Nothing is more united to a thing than its being, but God is not united to things: the first cause rules all things without being mixed with them (Liber de causis).
claims: The first cause is not mixed with the things it rules.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e227.summary: Second sed contra. Nothing has being except by participating divine being, the first being and cause of all being. What is participated is in the participant according to the participant's mode, since nothing receives beyond its measure. Every creature's mode is finite, so it receives finite being, inferior to divine being. So the being by which a creature formally exists is not divine being.
claims: What is participated is received according to the mode of the recipient.
Creaturely being, by which creatures formally exist, is finite and not divine being.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e230.summary: Thomas's determination. As Bernard says, God is the being of all things not essentially but causally. There are three kinds of agent cause. An equivocal cause shares neither name nor concept with its effect, as the sun makes heat without being hot. A univocal cause shares both, as man begets man. God acts in neither way: not univocally, since nothing agrees with him univocally; not equivocally, since cause and effect share name and concept by priority and posteriority, as God's wisdom makes us wise while ours always falls short of his, as accident falls short of being as it is in substance. So there is a third kind, the analogical agent. Divine being produces creaturely being in an imperfect likeness of itself, and divine being is called the being of all things as that from which all created being flows effectively and exemplarily.
claims: God is the being of all things causally, not essentially.
God is neither a univocal nor an equivocal cause but an analogical one.
All created being flows from divine being effectively and exemplarily, in imperfect likeness.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e233.summary: Reply to the Dionysian argument. It should be understood causally, as the word 'super-being' shows: if God were the creature's being essentially, he would not be super-being to the created.
claims: Dionysius's 'super-being' shows that God is the being of things only causally.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e239.summary: Reply to the second argument. Created being is not through something else if 'through' means an intrinsic formal cause, since by it the creature formally is. If 'through' means a formal cause outside the thing, or an efficient cause, then it is through divine being and not through itself.
claims: Created esse is the creature's intrinsic formal principle but exists through divine being as extrinsic exemplar and efficient cause.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e242.summary: Reply to the third argument. First things are diverse only by themselves, while what derives from them differs through the diversity of the firsts. Human and donkey differ by rational and irrational, which are not diversified by further differences but by themselves. Likewise God and created being differ not by differences added to both but by themselves, so they are properly called not 'different' but 'diverse'. 'Diverse' is absolute and 'different' relative (Metaphysics 10): whatever differs differs by something, but not everything diverse is diverse by something.
claims: God and created being are diverse by themselves, not different by added differences.
'Diverse' is absolute; 'different' implies something by which things differ.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e254.summary: First objection that 'He who is' is not first among divine names. What is prior should be treated first, and Dionysius treats the good before being in the Divine Names.
claims: Dionysius treats the good before being.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e260.summary: Second objection. The more common seems prior, and the good is more common than being. Divine being extends only to beings that participate being, but the good extends even to non-beings, which it calls into being ('bonum' from 'boare', to call, according to the commentator on Dionysius).
claims: The good extends even to non-beings.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e263.summary: Third objection. Of things equally simple, one is not prior to another. Being, true, good, and one are equally simple, since they are convertible.
claims: The transcendentals are equally simple and convertible.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e267.summary: Sed contra. According to Dionysius the divine attributes are known to us only from their participations in creatures, and among all participations being is first ('being is placed before his other participations'). This agrees with the Liber de causis: the first of created things is being. So in our understanding being is prior to the other attributes, and 'He who is' to the other names.
claims: Being is the first participation of God in creatures.
Prima rerum creatarum est esse.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e282.summary: Second sed contra. What is last in resolution is first in being, and being is last in the intellect's resolution, since when everything else is removed being remains.
claims: What is last in analysis is first in nature.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e285.summary: Thomas's determination. Being, good, one, and true simply precede the other divine names in our understanding, as their commonness shows. Compared among themselves, they can be taken by supposit, in which case they are convertible and inseparable, or by their concepts (intentiones), in which case being is simply prior. Being is included in the understanding of the others and not conversely. Being is the first thing to fall into the intellect's apprehension, without which nothing can be grasped, just as the first thing in its assent is the axioms, above all that contradictories are not simultaneously true. All the others are included in being, unitedly and indistinctly, as in a principle, which makes it most fitting as a divine name. The others add to being not a nature but a concept. One adds undividedness, a mere negation, and so is closest to being. True and good add relations: good to the end, true to the exemplar form (each thing is true by imitating the divine exemplar) or to a cognitive power, as true gold displays the form of gold and grounds a true judgment. Considered by causality, however, the good is prior, since it has the character of final cause, while being has only exemplary and efficient causality in God, and the end is the first of causes.
claims: Being, one, true, and good are convertible in supposit, but being is prior in concept.
Ens is the first thing grasped by the intellect, as the principle of non-contradiction is the first thing assented to.
One adds a negation to being; true and good add relations to exemplar or intellect and to the end.
In the order of causality the good is prior, as final cause, the cause of causes.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e288.summary: Reply to the first objection. Dionysius treats the divine names as they have the character of causality, as manifested in creatures' participation, and therefore treats the good before 'existing'.
claims: Dionysius orders the divine names by causality, where the good is first.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e291.summary: Reply to the second objection. The good is not more common in the range of predication, since there it converts with being, but in the character of its causality. Efficient and exemplary causality extends only to what actually participates the form of its exemplar cause, so the causality of being extends only to beings, and of life to the living. The causality of the end extends even to what does not yet participate the form, since imperfect things desire and tend toward an end they do not yet share, being on the way to it. Dionysius calls matter 'non-being' because of its attached privation, which is why he says that non-being itself desires the good.
claims: The good is more extensive than being not in predication but in final causality, which reaches what does not yet participate the form.
Matter is called non-being by reason of privation, and it desires the good.

ta-l1d8q1-d1e294.summary: Reply to the third objection. The transcendentals convert when considered by supposit, but by concept being is simpler and prior to the others.
claims: Convertible in supposit, the transcendentals are ordered in concept with being first.

ta-l1d8q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 8 lays out Lombard's plan for the remainder of Book I: essence, persons, and properties in themselves, and then compared. It places Distinction 8 as the treatment of the essence under truth, immutability, and simplicity, and announces inquiries into divine being and its measure, eternity.
claims: Book I treats essence, persons, and properties in themselves and then in relation.

ta-l1d8q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 asks whether being properly belongs to God. Against objections that being is common, that we name God only from creatures, that 'being' is as deficient as 'wisdom', and that the infinite is unnameable, Thomas holds that 'He who is' is God's most proper name. He gives four reasons: divine being is perfect, with nothing past or future (Jerome); we know only that God is, so we name him by indeterminate being (Damascene); being is the first participation and principle of the others (Dionysius); and in God alone being is the quiddity (Avicenna). The replies distinguish propriety as exclusivity from propriety as purity, and classify ways of naming God from creatures. 'He who is' is the least imperfect name, and the way of remotion ends in a darkness of ignorance beyond even creaturely being, in which we are best joined to God in this life.
claims: 'He who is' is the most proper name of God.
Being is proper to God as pure, unmixed with potentiality, though not exclusively his.
The way of remotion culminates in a darkness of ignorance beyond creaturely being.

ta-l1d8q1-Dd1e197.summary: Article 2 asks whether God is the being of all things. Against Dionysian and metaphysical arguments for identity, Thomas, with Bernard, holds that God is the being of all things causally, not essentially. He distinguishes equivocal, univocal, and analogical agents and identifies God as an analogical cause, from whom all created being flows effectively and exemplarily in imperfect likeness. Created being is the creature's intrinsic formal principle but exists through divine being as extrinsic cause. God and creature are 'diverse' by themselves rather than 'different' by added differences.
claims: God is the being of all things causally, not essentially.
God is an analogical agent, neither univocal nor equivocal.
God and creature are diverse by themselves, not different by a difference.

ta-l1d8q1-Dd1e246.summary: Article 3 asks whether 'He who is' is first among the divine names. Thomas holds that being, one, true, and good precede all other names. Among them, being is prior in concept, since it is the first thing grasped by the intellect and is included in all the others. One adds a negation, and true and good add relations to exemplar or intellect and to the end. In the order of causality, though, the good is first, as final cause, which explains why Dionysius treats it first and why it reaches even what does not yet participate being.
claims: Being is first in the order of concepts; the good is first in the order of causality.
Ens is the primum cognitum, included in all other concepts.

ta-l1d8q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 8 treats the propriety of divine being. The Prooemium lays out the plan of Book I (essence, persons, properties). Article 1 holds that 'He who is' is God's most proper name, by four arguments from Jerome, Damascene, Dionysius, and Avicenna, the last being that God alone has being as his quiddity. Being is proper to God not as exclusive but as pure, unmixed with potentiality, and the way of remotion ends in a darkness of ignorance in which we are best united to God in this life. Article 2 rejects the identification of God with the being of creatures. God is their being causally, as an analogical agent from whom created being flows effectively and exemplarily, and God and creature are diverse by themselves. Article 3 ranks the transcendentals: being is first in concept, the first thing the intellect grasps, while the good is first in causality as final cause.
claims: 'He who is' is the most proper name of God, since in him alone being is identical with quiddity.
God is the being of all things causally, not essentially, as an analogical agent.
Being is first in concept among the transcendentals; the good is first in causality.
